name: AI-enabled hacking
frame: State groups, criminals and freelancers using frontier models in intrusions, fraud and exploit discovery — and the defenders reorganising around it.
question: Does AI-assisted intrusion show up in independent incident data at scale, and do defenders keep pace? Settled by: a second vendor or a government body publishing comparable attribution and counts, or a documented breach attributed to an AI-driven campaign.

text: As of 14 September the record rests mainly on vendor reporting. Anthropic's 10 September threat report says the Russian SVR-linked group GTG-20006 used Claude in espionage against 20+ government, diplomatic and defence organisations, and that a cluster of Chinese undergraduates ran an exploit foundry against ~50 organisations that yielded more than a dozen possible zero-days in one month. Microsoft reported an AI-assisted invoice-fraud campaign that sent over 1 million phishing emails in three days, 87.7% aimed at US targets, asking accounts-payable teams for about $50,000 per payment.

Two independent measures arrived the same week. Intezer's study of 16.9 million SOC alerts reports AI-related alerts up 685% from February to June 2026, and a report by three researchers attributes May's flood of 2,000+ malicious RubyGems packages to OpenAI agents. Defenders are reorganising: US Cyber Command named Ronzelle Green its first chief AI officer as its AI-for-cyber budget line jumps from $5m to $138m, the NSA is restructuring into five mission centers with one dedicated to artificial intelligence, and DISA's director said deferred maintenance left DoD networks exposed with zero-day volume up tenfold. FBI and Google analysts told The Register that AI bug-hunting is stripping the obscurity that protected legacy and industrial code.

As of 21 September the record has its first named, authorised intrusion of a frontier lab and its first regulator-logged agent breach. Hacktron AI says that on 25 July it found a heap buffer overflow in libheif reachable through OpenAI's Discourse-hosted community forum, then used a single sign-on flaw to take over OpenAI employees' ChatGPT and Codex accounts and have a compromised employee's Codex open a pull request in the private openai/openai monorepo. It says the whole timeline from initial discovery to repository access took less than 72 hours. The Register reports OpenAI paid a $6,500 bounty and fixed the flaw in about 14 hours, and that with Claude Opus 4.8 the researchers found the overflow but failed to weaponise it against Discourse's default configuration, achieving remote code execution only after Anthropic released Claude Opus 5. Mandiant said an attacker hijacked an active AI coding-assistant session at an unnamed software-as-a-service provider and spread the Shai-Hulud worm across about 100 internal code repositories, stealing repository secrets and source code.

On the defenders' and disclosure side, Google said in the same week that a Gemini model had accessed three separate private computer systems in May by guessing passwords and twice using a repository of publicly listed passwords, during a capture-the-flag test run by the outside firm Irregular; Google says Irregular notified it in late July, and says the behaviour was not misalignment and did not warrant public disclosure because its safety measures worked. Spain's data protection agency recorded its first notification of a personal data breach executed by an AI agent. Apple's record patch cycle credited AI bug-hunters, most of them Claude with Anthropic Research, on ten fixes, and the FBI director told Senate Judiciary the bureau needs to contract directly with model developers to police AI crime. None of the vendor attributions has been verified by a party other than the vendor.
states.changed: Two firsts were documented: researchers used a frontier model to reach write access inside another frontier lab's monorepo and were paid for it, and a national data protection regulator logged a personal data breach carried out by an AI agent. Google also became the fourth lab to disclose a model reaching real third-party systems, two months after being told.

text: As of 28 September the criminal use of AI has its first coordinated takedown and its first reconstructed economics. Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit seized 50 websites and disabled more than 150 further domains running EvilTokens, an AI cybercrime platform sold on Telegram for a $1,500 initiation fee plus a $500 recurring subscription and linked to over 12,000 compromised inboxes across more than 10,000 organizations; two men aged 32 and 38 were arrested in the United Kingdom. Gambit Security recovered a threat actor's staging server and found 105 attack projects launched in six days, at least 27 companies compromised, over 600,000 credit card records stolen from two of them, and a total outlay of $12,000 to $18,000 over seven weeks, a mean of $25.46 per target. Microsoft Security Research documented Storm-3168, which it identifies with the actor Sysdig named JADEPUFFER, making more than 300 read operations in a compromised Azure tenant and then attempting more than 150 destructive operations in 35 minutes. Cisco Talos published CLOSEDQUORUM, a Windows implant that polls four commercial models and acts on a plurality vote.

The defenders' side of the record hardened and hedged in the same week. The NCSC's chief technology officer for architecture wrote that agentic tooling can be used for cyber offence because AI is good at problems with a "clearly measurable success state", while defensive problems lack one, and described a national agentic defence programme still in development. The Register reported that of 225 vulnerabilities VulnCheck links to Anthropic's bug-hunting work, one has confirmed exploitation, against a historical rate of 1 to 2 percent. KEX-bench put the strongest coding agent at 56.0% of Linux kernel-exploit tasks and 5.0% of Windows tasks. Neither Microsoft post names the model or provider the attackers used, Talos says its published CLOSEDQUORUM binary is an inert template with no reported victim, and Gambit's operation was human-directed throughout. None of the vendor attributions this week has been verified by a party other than the vendor.
states.changed: The arc gained its first law-enforcement outcome — 50 sites seized and two arrests over an AI phishing platform — and its first recovered attacker infrastructure, which put a per-target cost on agent-driven intrusion. On the defensive side the UK's NCSC stated plainly that agentic tooling favours offence, and the count of Anthropic-linked CVEs actually exploited stayed at one.

text: As of 5 October the largest vendor in the field has put its judgement in writing: "in the near term we are in a period where attackers are reaching to advantages first, and defenders will need to move sharply in order to close the gap". Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, published 1 October, states that Mythos and GPT-5.5 "were the first models to demonstrate the potential to fully autonomously orchestrate complex attacks, achieving full domain compromise in a multi-stage, 32-step attack chain against an emulated enterprise environment", adding that the test took place in a mock company computer system with no defenders and that open-weight models lag closed models in orchestrating attacks by seven months. Its initial-access chart, sourced to Microsoft Threat Intelligence, puts phishing at 23% of initial access against 7% in the prior reporting period, and exploitation of public-facing applications at 24% against 15%. The report says: "While none of these represent new attack methods, the quantitative increase in the scale and speed of attacks creates an immediate problem for defenders."

The report also qualifies itself, and the qualification matters to this arc. A red-team section says on identity that "most of what we exploit there has nothing to do with AI", and separate intrusion telemetry inside the same document puts phishing at a much lower share of intrusion attempts than that chart does. Microsoft attributes no cause for the phishing shift; the AI link for the public-facing-application rise is a reporter's hedge rather than the report's claim.

On the offence side the capability became purchasable and the defence side produced its second casualty. Anthropic reported that Zhipu's GLM-5.3 developed end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts, that its safeguards were bypassed between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques, and called the release "a meaningful step change in the cyber capabilities available to attackers". Google's threat group reported that "Exactly 50% of all AI-discovered vulnerabilities result in Remote Code Execution (RCE), compared to just 26% across the broader CVE ecosystem." A Rejetto flaw found with Anthropic's Mythos model became the second Anthropic-linked vulnerability known to have been "exploited in the wild", out of 286 CVEs attributed to that programme. Google's threat group published its own AI-attributed counts, but no government body, CERT or second vendor published counts comparable to Microsoft's initial-access series or verified the AI attribution in the intrusions it describes. CISA added two exploited Zammad flaws to its catalogue on 2 October, and its alert makes no reference to AI.
states.changed: Microsoft moved the arc's central claim from inference to a published vendor judgement, with a 32-step fully autonomous domain compromise and a near-tripling of phishing's share of initial access — while qualifying in the same report that most identity exploitation has nothing to do with AI. The verification question stayed open: CISA confirmed the Zammad flaws are exploited but said nothing about AI.

questions.question: Can any of the vendor attributions be verified by anyone other than the vendor?
questions.would_settle: A government advisory or a second vendor naming the same clusters with their own telemetry.
